wine.name: Barbár
wine.grapes: Cabernet Franc in the lead, with Merlot, Tannat and Kékfrankos; the shares move with the vintage.
wine.sites: Grown from the family's first vineyard, planted in 2002 on the crest of the Porkoláb valley on Szekszárd's loess, by the house's account; the Cabernet Franc of that ridge is the blend's backbone.
wine.making: Made only in vintages the family judges fully ripe and healthy. Each variety is raised apart for about a year in barrels of 300, 500 and 1,000 litres, mostly second and third fill with a small share of new oak, as the merchant's sheet for the 2020 vintage gives it; the blend then rests for over a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black cherry, blackcurrant and plum with cedar, tobacco leaf and black pepper; full and dense, Tannat giving firm, grippy tannin and Kékfrankos a lift of fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Firm in its youth and built by the house to age, it wants five years or more after release and a ripe vintage keeps for well over a decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Barbár is the Heimann family's flagship red from Szekszárd, a blend led by Cabernet Franc with Merlot, Tannat and Kékfrankos, made only in strong years. It is dense and firm, black cherry and pepper over grippy tannin, so decant it and pour it with red meat.
records.story: The Heimann family has lived in Szekszárd since 1758, by its own account, among the town's families of German descent who farmed its loess hills. The estate as a guest meets it is far younger. In 2002 the family planted its first vineyard of its own on the crest of the Porkoláb valley, and Barbár grew from it: a blend led by Cabernet Franc from that ridge, with Merlot, Tannat for grip and Kékfrankos for freshness, made only in vintages the family judges ripe and sound. It stands among Szekszárd's own named blends, a bigger and more intense cousin of the district's Bikavér. From 2005 the family planted a selection of Kadarka clones gathered from the district's old vineyards, the work that made the house a voice for the native grape, and the next generation, trained in Germany and France, carried it into single vineyard Kadarka and Kékfrankos under the Heimann & Fiai label, Heimann and Sons. The house turned towards organic farming from the middle of the 2010s, by its own account. In 2022 Barbarossa joined Barbár as its younger sibling, from the same four grapes. For a sommelier, Barbár shows what Szekszárd's loess gives Bordeaux varieties when Tannat and Kékfrankos sharpen the frame.

wine.name: Regnum
wine.grapes: Merlot and Cabernet Franc in the lead, with Cabernet Sauvignon and, from later vintages, Kékfrankos and Syrah; the mix moves with the year.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on Szekszárd's loess hills west of the Danube, where the warm southern climate ripens Bordeaux varieties fully.
wine.making: Made only in vintages the house judges strong. Fermented in tanks and aged in Hungarian and French oak barrels, about a year and a half by one merchant's sheet, the house aiming for fruit in front and the oak in the background; then blended and bottled.
wine.glass: Ripe plum, black cherry and blackcurrant with vanilla, clove and a touch of cocoa from the barrel; round and generous, Merlot's softness framed by Cabernet Franc's leafy freshness and fine tannin.
wine.ageing: Approachable a few years after release, it gains savoury depth over five to ten years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Regnum is Takler's Szekszárd blend in the Bordeaux manner, led by Merlot and Cabernet Franc and made only in strong years. Ripe plum and cassis over clove and soft, fine tannin show what the district's warmth gives these grapes; decant it for an hour.
records.story: The Taklers were a farming family of Szekszárd whose land was taken in the communist years. The modern estate began in 1996, when the founder, born into that family and by then a manager in the town's state economy, turned to wine. At first he sold to the local taverns, and soon to restaurants in Budapest, and with his two sons he steered the young estate towards bottled wines of quality. Regnum, Latin for kingdom, is the blend that set its course: Merlot and Cabernet Franc in the lead with Cabernet Sauvignon, raised in Hungarian and French oak and made only in vintages the house judges strong. In 2004 the founder was named Hungary's Winemaker of the Year. The family marked the estate's twentieth anniversary in 2016, and by then the range reached back to the district's own grapes as well: Kékfrankos from single hills, a Szekszárdi Bikavér named Örökség, heritage, and the old Kadarka, while Kékfrankos and Syrah joined Regnum's blend in later vintages. For a sommelier, Regnum is the bottle that shows Szekszárd's warm, round take on Bordeaux varieties, the style that made the district's modern name, set beside the native reds that have come back since.

wine.name: Nagyapám Kadarka
wine.grapes: Kadarka, Szekszárd's old native red grape, alone.
wine.sites: The selected fruit of the estate's old Kadarka vines in the family's valleys of Szekszárd, among them Bodzás, Görögszó, the Porkoláb valley and the Palánki hill, with vines from its own clone selection trials.
wine.making: Made to keep Kadarka's pale colour and perfume. The 2024 was fermented with its own yeasts and raised in stainless steel alone, with no barrel at all, while earlier vintages were raised in steel and oak together; the vessels move with the year.
wine.glass: Ripe cherry, raspberry and plum with black pepper and a hint of rose; light in colour and body, with soft tannin and a fresh, juicy line of acidity.
wine.ageing: Charming on release, it keeps its fruit for three to five years, the span the house gives one vintage, and gains a gentle savoury edge.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, cool like a light red; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

records.table: Nagyapám, My Grandfather, is Eszterbauer's Kadarka from Szekszárd, drawn from the family's old vines and its own clone trials. Pale and perfumed, all cherry, raspberry and pepper over soft tannin, it is the glass to pour when a guest asks what the district's native red tastes like.
records.story: Szekszárd's red wine owes much to settlers. Serbian refugees fleeing the Ottoman advance are thought to have brought Kadarka and the southern Slav way with red wine, and in the early eighteenth century, after the Ottoman wars, tax relief from the Benedictine abbots drew Hungarian and German families to replant the hills. The Eszterbauers appear in the town's vineyard records from 1746, and the family counts ten generations on its land. Kadarka became the district's grape, and after phylloxera ruined the vineyards in the later nineteenth century it was replanted widely. Some of those plantings survive: one of the family's Kadarka plots was set out in 1912 as bush vines. Kadarka later lost ground in the district, and its return has rested on growers who went back to such old vines. The Eszterbauers did so through clone selection trials on their own old plantings, and Nagyapám is the fruit of that work: the selected grapes of the old vines, made to keep the grape's pale colour and perfume. The name means my grandfather, and the family's labels carry its forebears, grandparents and great grandparents from the town's old middle class. For a sommelier, Nagyapám is a lesson in Kadarka itself: light, peppery and fresh, the old grape of Szekszárd in the glass.

wine.name: Valles Szekszárdi Bikavér Prémium
wine.classification: Prémium, the upper of the two tiers of Szekszárdi Bikavér
wine.grapes: Kékfrankos, about half, with Merlot, about a quarter, then Cabernet Franc and a little Kadarka; the mix moves with the year.
wine.sites: A blend across the family's valley vineyards, as its Latin name, valleys, suggests; the house's named sites include Hidaspetre and Bakta, on Szekszárd's loess.
wine.making: Raised in large oak casks of 1,000 to 1,500 litres for about seven tenths of the blend, the rest in new and used Hungarian barrels of 300 to 500 litres, as the house details the 2020 vintage. The Prémium rules then ask at least a year in oak and a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, ripe plum and blackberry with black pepper, clove and a savoury, smoky edge; medium bodied and elegant, the fresh acidity of Kékfrankos carrying fine, ripe tannin.
wine.ageing: Open a few years after release; a ripe vintage keeps and gains savoury depth for eight to ten years.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Valles is the Vida family's Prémium Szekszárdi Bikavér: about half Kékfrankos with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and a touch of Kadarka, raised mostly in large oak casks. Sour cherry and pepper over fine tannin make it the bottle to pour when a guest asks what Szekszárd's Bikavér is.
records.story: Bikavér, bull's blood, is a red of two towns. A drinking song of 1846 by a poet of Szekszárd praised the dark wine of its hills, but under communism Eger alone used the name, and Szekszárd won it back only at the end of the 1980s. The Vida family's estate began in those same years of change, at the turn of the 1990s, and grew into a family house of the district working Kadarka, Kékfrankos and Bikavér. In 2011 its founder was named Hungary's Winemaker of the Year. A son spent years at the estate replanting nearly all its vines and building a new cellar, and from the 2020 harvest a daughter, back from making wine in New Zealand, took charge of the cellar while her father kept to the vineyards: by the family's account a team of generations rather than one maker. Its single vineyard Kékfrankos from Hidaspetre shows one valley; Valles, Latin for valleys, gathers several into the Prémium tier of Szekszárdi Bikavér, the upper of the district's two, which asks lower yields and at least a year in oak and a year in bottle. For a sommelier, Valles is the clear answer to what Szekszárd's Bikavér is: Kékfrankos at its heart, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and the district's own Kadarka.

records.table: Porkolábvölgy is Vesztergombi's single vineyard Kékfrankos from the Porkoláb valley in Szekszárd, aged about two years in mid sized oak. Black cherry and pepper over a fresh, firm frame show what the district's leading grape gives on one site; decant it for an hour.
records.story: The Vesztergombi family traces its vines in Szekszárd to the early eighteenth century, by its own account, and a forebear served as the town's first vineyard judge, an office that brought a formal register of vineyard owners. The modern house is far younger. In 1991, as land taken under communism was handed back, the family recovered vines and a cellar on Kadarka Street and founded the business, and in 1993 its founder was named Hungary's Winemaker of the Year, early in the district's revival. The house grew around Bikavér and Kadarka, the wines that made its name, and later built a new winery on Borkút Street, where its reds are aged. Its St. László Bikavér, raised for two years in new oak barrels of 300 and 500 litres and then in bottle, was chosen among the wines of the Hungarian Parliament. Beside the blends, the family bottles Kékfrankos from single valleys, and the Porkoláb valley, a site several Szekszárd houses name on their labels, gives the one taught here: Kékfrankos alone, two years in oak. For a sommelier, it shows the district's leading grape on one site, firm, peppery and fresh, from a house that has worked these hills for generations.
